Both frameworks pick a render mode per route with one export in the route file. SSR: Zero export const renderMode = 'ssr', Next.js export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'. SSG: renderMode = 'ssg' against dynamic = 'force-static'. ISR: renderMode = 'isr' against revalidate = 60. Zero also has a per-route 'spa' mode, routeRules globs that set modes in one place, and mode: 'auto' (experimental), which infers each route's mode and prints the table at build.

Two stacks. React Native: your JavaScript bundle runs on the phone in the Hermes JavaScript engine, and React Native's renderer drives the platform widgets. Pyreon: your .tsx is compiled on your machine by PMTC into SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose source, Xcode and Gradle build a native binary, and the phone runs SwiftUI and Compose views with no JavaScript engine under the UI. The Pyreon native targets are labelled experimental.

The five migration steps as a loop: install the compat layer, change two config files, keep shipping, convert one component at a time, switch the compiler on. Six components of an app flip one by one from React-style (the body re-runs) to Pyreon (runs once) while @pyreon/react-compat sits underneath; at the last step the compat layer is switched off and jsxImportSource becomes @pyreon/core.

A loop of four steps. 1, the assistant writes a draft with two bugs that type-check: count(count() + 1) on line 9 and key={(i) => i.id} on a <For> on line 10. 2, the MCP validate tool returns two findings: signal-write-as-call on line 9 and for-with-key on line 10, both auto-fixable. 3, the fixes are applied: count.set(count() + 1) and by={(i) => i.id}. 4, pyreon check prints: no Pyreon anti-patterns in 1 file. Then the loop starts again with the next draft.

Left, the Counter you write: const count = signal(0), a span showing {count()} and two buttons. Middle, transformJSX. Right, what the compiler emits: a cached template string and one binding, _bindText(count, __t2). Below, the runtime wiring: clicking + calls count.update, the count signal notifies the one text node bound to it, and the number changes from 3 to 4; clicking - takes it back. A counter beside it reads Counter() ran 1×, and it never changes.

A precedence chain across the top: the page's own renderMode, the nearest _layout, routeRules, mode: 'auto' (experimental), then the app mode. Four routes resolve in turn. / falls through to the app mode and gets SSR. /about declares renderMode = 'ssg' on the page and gets SSG. /blog/** matches a routeRules glob and gets ISR. /admin/** matches routeRules and gets SPA.

Three browser frames. 1, the server-rendered HTML arrives with an empty email input; the JavaScript has not loaded. 2, the user types ada@pyreon before the JavaScript lands. 3, hydration adopts the existing nodes instead of replacing them: the typed text, the focus and the caret are all still there. Below, a dashed ghost frame shows the alternative, a hydration that rebuilds the DOM, where the input comes back empty and focus is lost.

One src/App.tsx feeds three lanes. Web: Vite builds it against @pyreon/runtime-dom into the DOM, with SSR and hydration. iOS: pyreon-native emits SwiftUI .swift files that Xcode builds into the app. Android: pyreon-native emits Compose .kt files that Gradle builds into the app. The iOS and Android lanes are labelled experimental. A trace runs down each lane in turn. A note says CI runs XCUITest on a Simulator and Compose tests on an emulator.
